technical-data.invention-title: DATA PROCESSING USING VARIOUS DATA PROCESSORS
TRAITEMENT DE DONNEES METTANT EN OEUVRE DIVERSES MACHINES DE TRAITEMENT DE DONNEES

abstract.p: A data processing arrangement includes various data processors (P) and a memory arrangement (MA) for applying input data (Di) to the data processors (P) and for storing output data (Do) from the data processors (P). The following steps are alternately carried out: a configuration step (CS) and a processing step (PS). In a configuration step (CS) the data processing arrangement is configured so that different respective data processors (P) process different blocks of data (B) contained in the memory arrangement (MA). In a processing step (PS), the blocks of data (B) are actually processed, whereas a data processor (P) stops when it has processed its block of data (B). Such a data processing arrangement offers great versatility, because different data processing chains can be realized without requiring relatively complicated software.

Un agencement de traitement de données comporte diverses machines de traitement de données (P) et un agencement de mémoires (MA) pour l'application de données d'entrée (Di) aux machines de traitement de données (P) et pour la mémorisation des données de sortie (Do) à partir des machines de traitement de données (P). On effectue les étapes suivantes: une étape de configuration (CS) et une étape de traitement. Dans une étape de configuration (CS) l'agencement de traitement de données est doté d'une configuration telle que les diverses machines de traitement respectives (P) traitent différents blocs de données (B) contenus dans l'agencement de mémoires (MA). Dans une étape de traitement (PS), les blocs de données (B) sont effectivement traitées, tandis qu'une machine de traitement (P) s'arrête lorsqu'elle a effectué son bloc de données (B). Un tel arrangement de traitement de données confère une grande versatilité, parce que diverses chaînes de traitement de données peuvent être réalisées sans avoir recours à des logiciels relativement complexes.

description.p: Data processing using various data processors.

The invention relates to a data processing arrangement which includes various data processors and a memory arrangement for applying input data to the data processors and for storing output data from the data processors. Such a data processing arrangement may be used, for example, in multimedia products.

EP-A-0,373,714 describes a data processor with a plurality of parallel-operating processor elements. A coupling network couples outputs of the data processor to its inputs. The coupling network includes the following components: one or more cross-bar switches and one or more arrays of silos. A series connection is formed in which these components are alternately arranged in a succession of at least three elements.
It is an object of the invention to allow greater versatility of a data processing arrangement as defined in the opening paragraph.

The invention takes the following aspects into consideration. Let it be assumed that the data processing arrangement processes data in the following manner. A first data processor processes the data so as to obtain once processed data which is written into the memory arrangement. Subsequently, a second data processor reads the once processed data, processes it so as to obtain twice processed data which is written into the memory arrangement, and so on. That is, the data processors form a data processing chain. The memory arrangement provides buffer storage capacity between two successive data processors in the data processing chain.

The data processing as described hereinbefore involves a potential synchronization problem. A data processor may request data from the memory arrangement, whereas this data has not yet been written into the memory arrangement by a preceding data processor in the data processing chain. This synchronization problem is due to processing delays of the various data processors, or due to different processing speeds, or both.
In the background art the synchronization problem appears to be solved in the following manner. Each data processor is programmed such that it takes into account the processing delays and the processing speeds of preceding data processors. That is, the programming of a data processor includes correct timing of the data processing in the data processor with respect to the data processing in the preceding data processors.

The solution to the synchronization problem as described hereinbefore has the following drawback. Let it be assumed that a different data processing chain is desired. This implies that the order in which the data processors process data needs to be changed, or that one or more data processor need to carry out a different type of processing, or both. In that case the processing delays of one or more data processors will change, or the processing speeds of one or more data processors will change, or both. Consequently, it will be necessary to re-program almost every data processor in order to avoid a synchronization problem. This re-programming will generally be quite complex, because a data processor has to take into account the processing delays and the processing speeds of various other data processors. This is true even if only a single data processor is made to carry out different data processing. Thus, the background-art data processing arrangement is ill suited for realizing different data processing chains because this requires relatively complicated software.

In accordance with the invention, a data processing arrangement as defined in the opening paragraph is controlled in the following manner. A configuration step and a processing step are alternately carried out. In the configuration step, the data processing arrangement is configured so that different respective data processors process different blocks of data contained in the memory arrangement. In the processing step, the blocks of data are actually processed, whereas a data processor stops when it has processed its block of data. Thus, according to the invention it can be prevented that, while the data processors process data, a data processor requests data from the memory arrangement which an other data processor has not yet written into the memory arrangement. Thus, the synchronization problem is solved. What is more, while the data processors process data, a data processor need not have knowledge of the processing delays and the processing speeds of the other data processors. Consequently, if the order in which the data processors process data is changed, it will not be necessary to re-program almost every data processor for reasons of synchronization. Furthermore, if a data processor is re-programmed to carry out a different type of processing, it will not be necessary to re-program various others data processors. Consequently, a data processing arrangement in accordance with the invention can realize
different data processing chains without requiring relatively complicated software. Thus, the invention offers greater versatility.
The invention and additional features, which may be optionally used to implement the invention to advantage, are apparent from and elucidated with reference to the drawings described hereinafter.

Fig. 1 is a conceptual diagram illustrating basic features of the invention as claimed in claim 1. Figs. 2 and 3 are conceptual diagrams illustrating additional features as claimed in claims 2 and 3, respectively.
Fig. 4 is a block diagram illustrating an example of a data processing arrangement in accordance with the invention.
Fig. 5 is a table illustrating an example of a data flow in the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig.3.
Fig. 6 is a block diagram illustrating an example of a control register in the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4.

Fig. 7 is a flow chart diagram illustrating a method of operation of the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4. Fig. 8 is a time diagram illustrating signals associated with the method illustrated in Fig. 7.
Fig. 9 is a block diagram illustrating an example of a memory block in the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4.
Fig. 10 is a binary- word diagram illustrating a memory-read control word for the memory block illustrated in Fig. 9.

First, some remarks will be made on the use of reference signs. Similar entities are denoted by an identical letter code throughout the drawings. Various similar entities may be shown in a single drawing. In that case, a numeral is added to the letter code so as to distinguish similar entities from each other. The numeral will be between parentheses if the number of similar entities is a running parameter. In the description and the claims, any numeral in a reference sign may be omitted if appropriate.
Fig. 1 illustrate basic features of the invention. A data processing arrangement includes various data processors P and a memory arrangement MA for applying input data Di to the data processors P and for storing output data Do from the data processors P. The following steps are alternately carried out: a configuration step CS and a processing step PS. In a configuration step CS, the data processing arrangement is configured so that different respective data processors P process different blocks of data B contained in the memory arrangement MA. In a processing step PS, the blocks B of data are actually processed whereas a data processor P stops when it has processed its block of data. Fig. 1 additionally illustrates that a subsequent configuration step CS will generally be carried out when each data processor P has processed its block B of data ( VP: B=PROC = CS).

To advantageously implement the features illustrated in Fig. 1, the following aspects have been taken into consideration. There are various manners in which it can be achieved that a configuration step CS will generally be carried out only when each data processor P has processed its data. A basic manner is as follows. A configuration step is carried out a fixed number of clock cycles after the previous configuration step. That is, there is a fixed time slot for the processing step in between these configuration steps. The data processing arrangement can be configured such that each data processor P will certainly be able to carry out its data processing within the fixed time slot.

For reasons of reliability, the fixed time slot as described above should preferably include a certain margin. This to ensure that the last data processor has finished its processing before a new configuration step is carried out. It may happen that this margin turns out to be relatively large for some processing steps. That is, it may happen that each data processor has finished its processing well before the configuration step is carried out. In that case, the data processing arrangement will, in effect, be idle during a certain number of clock cycles. Clock cycles are, as it were, wasted. Thus, the method described hereinbefore has a drawback in terms of processing speed.

Fig. 2 illustrates the following features which may be optionally added to the features which have been discussed with reference to Fig. 1. In the processing step PS, a data processor P provides an end-of-processing indication PEI when the data processor P has processed its block of data (B=PROC). It is monitored whether each data processor P which processed a block of data has provided an end-of-processing indication PEI (VP:PEI?). If so (VP:PEI), a new configuration step CS is carried out.

The features illustrated in Fig. 2 provide the following advantage. A configuration step can be carried out shortly after each data processor P has finished its data
processing. For example, the configuration step may be carried out at the first clock cycle following the instant at which each data processor has provided an end-of-processing indication PEI. There is no need to build in a margin as in the method described before the description of Fig.2. Thus, the Fig. 2 features allow a greater percentage of clock cycles to be effectively used for data processing. Consequently, the features illustrated in Fig. 2 contribute to a satisfactory processing speed.

To advantageously implement the features illustrated in Fig. 1 , the following aspects have also been taken into consideration. In practice, the data processing arrangement will comprise an assembly of controllable circuits which includes the data processors. A controllable circuit will typically include a control register whose content defines the operation of the controllable circuit. In a configuration step, it is possible to serially write configuration data into various control registers so as to obtain the desired configuration for the subsequent processing step. However, this may be relatively time consuming if there are relatively many controllable circuits and hence potentially many control registers to be written. In that case, the configuration step will be relatively lengthy. As a result, the percentage of time during which the data processing arrangement effectively processes data will be relatively low, because the data processing arrangement does not process data during a configuration step. Thus, the data processing arrangement will have a relatively low processing speed.

Fig. 3 illustrates the following features which may be optionally added to the features which have been discussed with reference to Fig. 1. In a processing step PS, configuration data CD is written into a front register FREG associated with a controllable circuit CC. In a configuration step CS, the configuration data CD is transferred from the front register FREG to a shadow register SREG, the content of the shadow registers SREG defining the operation of the controllable circuit CC. The features illustrated in Fig. 3 provide the following advantage.

Configuration data CD in a front register FREG does not immediately influence the operation of the controllable circuit CC whith which the front register FREG is associated. Thus, during a processing step PS[i], configuration data CD for the next processing step PS[i+l] can be send in advance to the front registers FREG of various controllable circuits. This sending of configuration data CD can be done serially via a bus system, which is advantageous in terms of circuit complexity. The data processing arrangement can be configured for the next processing step PS[i+l] by transferring configuration data CD contained in front registers FREG to shadow registers SREG. These transfers can be done in parallel, for example, within one clock cycle. Thus, the features illustrated in Fig. 3 allow a configuration step to be carried
out relatively fast such that a relatively high percentage of time can effectively be used for data processing. Consequently, the features illustrated in Fig. 3 contribute to a satisfactory processing speed.

Fig. 4 illustrates an example of a data processing arrangement which includes the features illustrated in the Figs. 1, 2 and 3. The data processing arrangement receives data to be processed via a bi-directional bus HGHWY and outputs processed data via the same bus. The data processing arrangement includes a master control processor MCP and an assembly of functional units: a bus interface IF, memory blocks MB, a write crossbar XB/W, a read crossbar XB/R and data processors P. The read crossbar XB/W and the write crossbar XB/R define connections between the bus interface IF and the data processors P on the one hand and the memory block MB on the other hand.

Fig. 5 illustrates an example of a method of operation of the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4. In Fig. 5, each column represents a processing steps PS and each rows represents a block of data B to be processed. In a processing step PS[i], the bus interface IF fetches a block of data B[j] to be processed from the bi-directional bus HGHWY and writes this data into one of the memory blocks MB, for example the memory block MBl (PS[i]/B[j]: HGHWY→IF→MBl). In the processing step PS[i+l], the block of data is read by one of the data processors P, for example the data processor PI, and processed by this data processor. Accordingly, a block of once processed data is obtained which is written into one of the memory blocks MB, for example the memory block MB2 (PS[i+l]/B[j]:

MBl— »P1→MB2). In the processing step PS[i+2], the once processed data is subsequently read by another data processor P, for example the data processor P2, and processed by this data processor. Accordingly, a block of twice processed data is obtained which is written into one of the memory blocks, for example the memory block MB3 (PS[i+2]/Bβ]: MB2- P2— MB3). This processing may continue in the same fashion until the block of data B[j] has been N times processed, N being an integer. The bus interface IF may then place the N times processed block of data on the bi-directional bus HGHWY.

In the processing step PS[i+l], the bus-interface IF fetches a new block of data B[j+1] from the bi-directional bus HGHWY and writes this data into one of the memory blocks MB, for example the memory block MBl (PS[i+l]/B[j+l]: HGHWY→IF→MBl). In the processing step PS[i+2], the block of data is read by one of the data processors P, for example the data processor PI, and processed by this data processor. Accordingly, a block of once processed data is obtained which is written into one of the memory blocks MB, for example the memory block MBl (PS[i+2]/B[j+2]: MB1→P1-»MB2). Thus, the same data
processing chain applied to the data block B[j] may also be applied to the data block Bβ+1]. However, the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 1 also allows a different data processing chain to be applied to the data block B j+lJ.

The master control processor MCP determines which data processing chain is applied to a certain block of data being fetched from the bi-directional bus HGHWY. The master control processor MCP also determines the amount of data which a processor P should process during a processing step PS. To that end, the master control processor MCP applies configuration data CD to the various functional units. For example, the configuration data CD which the master control processor MCP applies to the read crossbar XB/R defines connections between the outputs of the memory blocks MB on the one hand and the processors P and the bus interface on the other hand.

The configuration data CD which the master control processor MCP applies to a processor P defines the type of data processing to be carried out by the processor P. For example, let it be assumed that the processor P is a convolution filter. In that case the configuration data CD defines the filter characteristics, that is, it defines the size of the filter kernel and the filter coefficients. The configuration data CD also defines the number of data elements, for example pixels, which the processor P has to process during a processing step PS. This will be explained in greater detail hereinafter.

Fig. 6 illustrates a control register in which the master control processor MCP may write configuration data CD. Each functional unit has one or more of such control registers. The control registers are coupled to the master control processor MCP via an internal control-data bus ICB and an internal address bus IAB. The control register includes an address decoder ADEC, a front register FREG and a shadow register SREG. The control register may optionally include a selector SEL which is shown in broken lines. The front register FREG has an input I which is coupled to the internal control-data bus ICB, and an output O which is coupled to an input of the shadow register SREG. An output O of the shadow register SREG is coupled to one or more controllable elements in the functional unit to which the control register belongs, Thus, the content of the shadow register SREG determines the operation of the functional unit. The master control processor MCP writes configuration data CD into a control register in the following manner. The master control processor MCP places configuration data CD for the control register on the internal control-data bus ICB. It also places address data AD on the internal address bus IAB. On the basis of the address data AD the address decoder ADEC of the control register determines whether the configuration data CD is intended for the
control register. If so, the address decoder ADEC applies an enable signal EN to the front register FREG. In response, the front register FREG loads the configuration data CD present on the internal control-data bus ICB. The configuration data CD is further transferred to the shadow register SREG by means of a load configuration command LC. If the load configuration command LC is applied to the shadow register SREG, this register takes over the configuration data CD previously stored in the front register FREG.

It should be noted that the selector SEL, shown in broken lines, allows the content of the shadow register SREG to be transferred back to the front-register FREG. That is, if a swap command SWP is applied to the selector SEL, the front register FREG takes over the content of the shadow register SREG and vice versa. This feature allows the functional unit to carry out two different types of operation in an alternating fashion without this requiring a transfer of configuration data CD via the internal control-data bus ICB upon each alternation.

Fig. 7 illustrates a method of operation of the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4. There are two steps which are alternately carried out: a configuration step CS and a processing step PS. Data which has been fetched from the bi-directional bus HGHWY is processed only during a processing step PS, but not during a configuration step CS. The content of the shadow registers SREG belonging to the various functional units can be modified only during a configuration step CS, but not during a processing step PS. In a configuration step CS, the master control processor MCP provides a load configuration command LC for the control registers CREG of the functional units. As explained with reference to Fig. 6, the configuration data CD contained in the front register FREG will be transferred to the shadow register SREG (CD: FREG→SREG). As a result, each functional unit will be configured in accordance with the configuration data CD which the master control processor has previously transferred to the control register CREG of the functional unit.

In a processing step PS, the functional units process data which has previously been fetched from the bi-directional bus HGHWY. Typically, a block B of data contained in a memory block MB is transferred to a data processor P via the read crossbar XB/R. The data processor P processes the data and the data thus processed is transferred via the write crossbar XB/W to a certain portion of a memory block MB (B: MB→XB/R->P→XB/W→MB). Meanwhile, the master control processor MCP may write configuration data CD into the front registers FREG of one or more functional units (CD: MCP→FREG). That is, during a
processing step PS, the master control processor MCP can, as it were, prepare a new configuration for the next processing step PS.

Fig. 8 illustrates how a processing step PS[i-l] is succeeded by a configuration step CS[i] and a new processing step PS[i]. In Fig. 8, four binary signals are represented: a start signal STS, a configuration-done signal CDS, a load-configuration signal LCS and an end-of-operation signal EOS. The start signal STS originates from the master control processor MCP and is applied to the data processors P (MCP→P: STS). The configuration- done signal CDS originates from a functional unit, for example a processor P. Each functional unit having a control register generates a configuration-done signal CDS and applies this signal to the master control processor MCP (P,XB,MB,IF→MCP: CDS . The load- configuration signal LCS originates from the master control processor MCP and is applied to the various functional units (MCP- P,XB,MP,IF: LCS). The end-of-operation signal EOS originates from a data processor P. Each data processor P generates an end-of-operation signal EOS and applies this signal to the master control processor MCP (P→MCP: EOS). Fig. 8 also shows a clock signal CLK with rising edges 1-8. With each rising edge a clock-controlled element in the data processing arrangement may change its state.

Let it be assumed that the signals illustrated in Fig. 8 are exchanged between the master control processor MCP and the data processor PI. At the rising edge 1 of the clock signal CLK, the data processor PI has finished its task. In order to signal this to the master control processor MCP, the data processor PI causes its end-of-operation signal EOS to change from '0' to ' 1 '. A data processor P may know that it has finished its task, for example, by means of a counter which is loaded in a configuration step and counts down one unit with each processed data element in a processing step. When the counter has reached zero, the data processor P has processed the required number of data elements and, consequently, it stops processing and causes its end-of-operation signal EOS to change from '0' to ' 1 '.

It is assumed that all end-of-operation signals EOS are ' 1 ' at the rising edge 3 of the clock signal CLK. The master control processor MCP deduces from this, as it were, that all data processors P have finished their tasks. In response, the master control processor MCP causes the load configuration signal LCS to change from '0' to ' 1 ' at the rising edge 4 of the clock signal CLK. In response to the load configuration signal LCS becoming ' 1 ', the configuration data CD in the front register FREG is transferred to the shadow register SREG. This has been explained hereinbefore with reference to the FigS 5 and 6.

The data processor PI causes its configuration-done signal CDS to change from '0' to ' 1 ' at the rising edge 5. By doing so, the data processor PI confirms to the master
control processor MCP that the configuration data CD has been transferred and hence that it is ready to carry out its new task. It is assumed that all configuration-done signals CDS have changed from '0' to ' 1 ' at the rising edge 5.

The master control processor MCP causes the load configuration signal LCS to change from ' 1 ' back to '0' at the rising edge 5. In response to the load configuration signal LCS be coming '0', each data processor P causes its end-of-operation signal EOS to changes from ' 1 ' to back to '0' at the rising edge 6. That is, a reset of the load configuration signal LCS triggers a reset of the end-of operation signal EOS at the next rising edge of the clock signal CLK. It is assumed that all configuration-done signals CDS are ' 1 ' at the rising edge

6. The master control processor MCP deduces from this, as it were, that all functional units are ready to carry out a new processing step. Accordingly, the master control processor MCP causes the start signal STS to change from '0' to ' 1 ' at the rising edge 6. In other words, the master control processor MCP gives the start signal for a new processing step at the rising edge 6. In response to the start signal STS be coming ' 1 ', the functional units will start to carry out the tasks they have been assigned to do by means of the configuration data CD.

The master control processor MCP causes the start signal STS to change from ' 1 ' back to '0' at the rising edge 7. In response to the start signal be coming '0', each functional unit causes its configuration-done signal CDS to change from T back to '0' at the rising edge 8. That is, a reset of the start signal STS triggers a reset of the configuration-done signal CDS at the next rising edge of the clock signal CLK.

Fig. 9 illustrates a memory block MB of the data processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4. The memory block MB includes a memory controller MCTRL and a multi-memory arrangement MMA composed of five static random-access memories SRAM1- SRAM5. The multi-memory arrangement MMA has an input port for receiving output data Do from a data processor P[i] via the write crossbar XB/W. The multi-memory arrangement also has an output port for applying input data Di to a data processor P[j] via the read crossbar XB/R.

The memory block MB basically operates as follows. The memory controller MCTRL instructs the multi-memory arrangement MMA as to in which SRAM the output data Do has to be written and at which address. It does so by means of a write-page selection signal PG/W and a write address AD/W. The memory controller MCRTL also instructs the multi- memory arrangement MMA as to from which SRAM input data Di has to be read and at which address. It does so by means of a read-page selection signal PG/R and a read address AD/R. A
static SRAM memory can either be written or read at a given instant. Thus, writing and reading cannot be carried out simultaneously in a static SRAM. The memory controller MCTRL ensures that the SRAM selected for writing is not the same as the SRAM selected for reading. During a configuration step, the master control processor MCP applies configuration data CD to the memory controller MCTRL. The configuration data CD for the memory controller MCTRL can be seen as a set of initialization commands allowing it to autonomously generate the signals PG/W, AD/W, PG/R and AD/R during the processing step which follows. Accordingly, the configuration data CD for the memory controller MCTRL indicates where reading should start, which SRAM and which address, and how reading should continue. The configuration data CD also indicates where writing should start, which SRAM and which address, and how writing should continue.

During a processing step, the data processor P[i] applies next- write commands NXT/W to the memory controller MCTRL. A next-write command NXT/W indicates that the data processor P[i] is ready to write a data element into the multi-memory arrangement MMA. The data processor P[j] applies next read commands NXT/R to the memory controller MCTRL. A next-read command NXT/W indicates that the data processor P[j] is ready to read a data element from the multi-memory arrangement MMA. The memory controller MCTRL increments the write address AD/W and the read address AD/R in response to the next-write command NXT/W and the next-read command NXT/R, respectively. To that end, the memory controller MCTRL may include two loadable counters, one for the write address AD/W and one for the read address AD/R, the counters receiving the next-write command NXT/W and the next-read command NXT/R, respectively, as increment-instructions.

Fig. 10 illustrates a memory-read control word MRC W which may form part of the configuration data CD for the memory block MB illustrated in Fig. 9. It is assumed that the memory controller MCTRL includes a read-address counter. The memory-read control word MRCW comprises 8 bits: b[7]-b[0]. The function of these bits will now be explained.

Bit b[7] is a read keep-page flag KPF. When this flag is set to '0' the read-page selection PG/R is automatically incremented when the read-address counter overflows. When the read-address counter overflows while the read-page selection PG/R has its maximum value, the read-page selection PG/R is set to its minimum value. This can be regarded as a wrap around. When the read keep-page flag KPF is set to "1", the read -page selection PG/R is not changed during a processing step.

Bit b[6] has no special function.
Bits b[5]-b[3] constitute a 3-bit page-read value PRN. The page-read value PRV indicates the starting value for the read-page selection PG/R and hence indicates from which SRAM data the reading of data should start.

Bits b[2] and b[l] constitute a read-mode value RMV. The read-mode value RMV determines which read mode is to be applied. There are four read modes. In a first read mode, the content of the read-address counter is reset in response to a load configuration command LC. In a second read mode, the reading starts at an address which the master control processor MCP has applied to the memory controller MCTRL. In a third read mode, the reading starts at an address currently contained in the read-address counter. The read-page selection PG/R is maintained at its current value. That is, the page-read value PRV is ignored. In a fourth read mode, the reading starts at an address currently contained in the read-address counter, but the read-page selection is set in accordance with the page-read value PRV. Bit b[0] is a read-enable flag EΝF. When this flag is set to '0', reading is allowed. When the read-enable flag EΝF flag is set to ' 1 ', the 8-bit counter is not incremented, not even if the memory controller MCTRL receives a next-read command ΝXT/R.
Furthermore, the other bits of the memory-read control word MRCW, bits b[7]-b[l], are ignored.

It goes without saying that the configuration data CD for the memory block MB illustrated in Fig. 9 may include a memory-write control word similar to the memory-read control word MRCW illustrated in Fig. 10.

In summary, the processing arrangement illustrated in Fig. 4 operates as follows. In a configuration step, the master control processor MCP configures each data processor P to carry out a certain type of processing. For example, in a video processing application a data processor P may be a horizontal filter or a vertical filter whose characteristics, such as the number of filter taps and filter coefficients, are defined by the configuration data CD. The master control processor MCP, further more, configures each data processor P to process a given number of data elements, for example, a given number of pixels. Accordingly, the master control processor MCP configures the data processor P to provide the necessary number of next-read and next-write commands ΝXT/R, ΝXT/W. The master control processor MCP also configures the write crossbar XB/W and the read crossbar XB/R. Accordingly, for each data processor P it is defined from which memory block MB the data processor P will read input data Di and in which memory block MB the data processor P will write output data Do. The master control processor MCP also configures each memory block MB. Accordingly, for a data processor P which is to read input
data Di from the memory block MB, the master control processor MCP defines the SRAM and the address at which reading will start. That is, the master control processor MCP defines, as it were, which portion of data contained in the memory block MB is to be processed for the data processor P which is to write output data Do into the memory block MB, the master control processor MCP also defines the SRAM and the address at whichwriting will start. That is, the master control processor MCP defines, as it were, in which portion of the memory block MB processed data is to be written.

Once the master control processor MCP has configured the functional elements as described hereinbefore, it provides a start command which marks the beginning of a processing step. In the processing step, the functional elements operate autonomously. Their configuration as defined in the configuration step is maintained. The master control processor MCP waits, as it were, until each data processor P has processed the amount of data it has been instructed to process. When each data processor P has finished its task, which marks the end of the processing step, the master control processor MCP may carry out a new configuration step.

Thus, the master control processor MCP can be seen as an orchestrator who assigns tasks to the various functional units, who lets the functional units carry out their tasks, and who waits until the last one has finished its task before assigning any new task. The master control processor MCP keeps track, as it were, of a block of data which has been fetched from the bi-directional bus HGHWY. That is, with each configuration step, the master control processor MCP knows what processing the block of data has already undergone, where the block of data processed thus far is stored, and what processing needs yet to be carried out before the block of data can be outputted via the bi-directional bus.

The drawings and their description hereinbefore illustrate rather than limit the invention. It will be evident that there are numerous alternatives which fall within the scope of the appended claims. In this respect, the following closing remarks are made.

With reference to Fig. 1 it has been said that a data processor stops when it has processed its block of data. This, however, does not mean that it will then always be completely idle until a new processing step begins. For example, while the data processor waits for the other data processors to have processed their blocks of data, it may process internal data or any other data that does not belong to the data to be processed contained in the memory arrangement.

There are various manners to configure a data processing arrangement in accordance with the invention. In a configuration step, it is possible to configure the data
processing arrangement so that all data processors process a block of data in the processing step which follows. However, it is also possible to configure the data processing arrangement so that some data processors process a block of data whereas the rest of the data processors do not. Thus, in a configuration step, it is possible to define a group of data processors that are active in the processing step which follows. The group of active data processors may vary in composition from one processing step to another. For example, let it be assumed that a data processing arrangement comprises three data processors: A, B and C. It is possible that in a processing step all three data processors are active, whereas in a subsequent processing step only data processors A and B are active and in a yet subsequent processing step data processors B and C are active.

There are numerous manners in which the memory arrangement can be implemented. Fig. 4 illustrates only one possible implementation in which the memory arrangement is formed by a plurality of memory blocks. This by no means excludes other possible implementations such as, for example, an implementation in which the memory arrangement is formed by a single physical memory circuit.

There are numerous ways in which a data processor arrangement can be made to operate in accordance with the basic principles illustrated in Fig. 1. For example, referring to the implementation illustrated in Fig. 4, a set of instructions stored on a computer usable medium, such as, for example, a disk, can be loaded into a program memory of the master control processor MCP. The set of instructions causes the master control processor MCP to carry out the operations described with reference to Figs. 5-10.

There are numerous ways of physically spreading functions or functional elements over various units. In this respect, the drawings are very diagrammatic, each representing only one possible embodiment of the invention. Thus, although a drawing shows different functional elements as different blocks, this by no means excludes that some functional elements, or all functional elements, may be implemented as a single physical unit. Any reference sign in a claim should not be construed as limiting the claim.

claim.claim-text: 1. A method of controlling a data processing arrangement which includes various data processors (P) and a memory arrangement (MA) for applying input data (Di) to the data processors and for storing output data (Do) from the data processors (P), characterized in that the following steps are alternately carried out: a configuration step (CS) in which the data processing arrangement is configured so that different respective data processor (P) process different blocks of data (B) contained in the memory arrangement (MA); and a processing step (PS) in which the blocks of data (B) are actually processed, whereas a data processor (P) stops when it has processed its block of data.

2. A method as claimed in claim 1 , characterized in that a processing step (PS) includes the sub-steps of: providing an end-of-processing indication (PEI) when a data processor (P) has processed a block of data (B); and - monitoring whether the different respective data processors (P) have all provided an end-of-processing indication (PEI) and, if so, proceeding to a new configuration step (CS).

3. A method as claimed in claim 1, characterized in that a processing step (PS) includes the sub-step of: writing configuration data (CD) into a front register (FREG) associated with a controllable circuit (CC); and in that a configuration step (CS) comprises the sub-step of: transferring configuration data (CD) from the front register (FREG) to a shadow register (SREG), the content of the shadow registers (SREG) defining the operation of the controllable circuit (CC).

4. A data processing arrangement which includes various data processors (P) and a memory arrangement (MA) for applying input data (Di) to the data processors and for storing
output data (Do) from the data processors (P), characterized in that the data processing arrangement includes a controller (MCP) for alternately carrying out the following steps: a configuration step (CS) in which the data processor arrangement so that different respective data processors (P) process different blocks of data (B) contained in the memory arrangement (MA); and an initiation step (INIT) in which the different respective data processors are initiated to process the different blocks of data (B).

5. A data processing arrangement as claimed in claim 4, characterized in that the different respective data processors (P) are arranged for providing an end-of-processing indication (PEI) when the data processor (P) has processed its block of data (B), the controller (MCP) being arranged for proceeding to a new configuration step (CS) when the different respective data processors (P) have all provided an end-of-processing indication (PEI).

6. A data processing arrangement as claimed in claim 4, characterized in that the data processing arrangement includes a plurality of controllable circuits (CC), a controllable circuit having a front register (FREG) and a shadow register (SREG), the content of the shadow register (SREG) defining the operation of the controllable circuit (CC), the controller (MCP) being arranged for writing configuration data (CD) in the front register (FREG) during the processing of the blocks of data (B) and for causing the configuration data (CD) to be transferred from the front register (FREG) to the shadow register (SREG) during a configuration step (CS).

7. A computer program product for controlling a data processing arrangement which includes various data processors (P) and a memory arrangement (MA) for applying input data (Di) to the data processors and for storing output data (Do) from the data processors (P), characterized in that the computer program product comprises a set of instructions which, when loaded into the data processing arrangement, causes the data processing arrangement to carry out the method as claimed in claim 1.
